caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real?

On 16 October 1869, two men hired to dig a well behind William Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, struck a ten-foot stone man. Newell put a tent over the hole and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute look. Three to five hundred people came a day.

It was made by Newell's cousin, George Hull, a tobacconist who had lost an argument with a preacher about the giants named in Genesis. He had a gypsum block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling the workmen it was for a Lincoln monument, then had it carved in Chicago in his own likeness. Sand, sulphuric acid and a board of steel knitting needles aged the skin and made the pores. Total cost: $2,600.

Geologists saw through it fast. Yale's Othniel Marsh called it "a most decided humbug" — soluble gypsum buried for centuries would not still carry fresh tool marks. Hull confessed on 10 December 1869, and in February 1870 a court declared both his giant and P. T. Barnum's plaster copy fakes.

Still unresolved: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter who took the job, knew what he was making. And a Michigan arcade owner says the copy displayed there is Barnum's.

Images: Bain News Service (1910); a Popular Graphic Arts lithograph of "The Onondaga Giant"; and both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa. All public domain.
